title: Hearing the unhearable
teaches: How a heterodyne detector mixes a bat's call down into hearing, how to tune one, and how to build one on a breadboard
summary: **A bat's call is loud but too high to hear.** Calls reach 120 decibels or more close to the bat's mouth, at 20 to 100 kHz, above the 15 to 20 kHz where human hearing stops.

**A heterodyne detector multiplies, it does not slow down.** The microphone's signal is multiplied by a tone the detector makes itself, which produces the sum and the difference of the two frequencies.
**Only the difference reaches the speaker.** A filter passes the difference when it is under about 5 kHz, so you hear a band about 10 kHz wide around the dial, live.
**An FM sweep crosses that window in a millisecond or two.** It comes out as a tick or a fuller "tock", loudest when the dial sits where the call lingers, near its end.
**A constant-frequency call becomes a steady whistle.** Its pitch is the gap between call and dial, and it falls to nothing at zero beat, when the two agree.
**The dial tells you roughly who is calling.** Myotis over water sound best near 40 to 50 kHz, big brown and silver-haired bats near 25 to 30.
**The idea came from radio.** Reginald Fessenden used it to make inaudible radio waves audible in the early 1900s, and named it heterodyne, "other force".
**A working detector is six blocks.** Microphone, preamplifier, mixer, oscillator, low-pass filter and amplifier, all common parts on a breadboard.

blocks.text: Stand on the path around a lake at dusk in July and the air over the water is full of bats, turning and dropping a metre above the surface. They are shouting. A hunting bat's call, measured ten centimetres in front of its mouth, can pass 120 decibels, as loud as a smoke alarm right beside your ear. Yet the lake is quiet. The calls are at 40,000 to 90,000 vibrations a second, written 40 to 90 **kilohertz** (kHz), and human hearing stops at about 20 kHz in a child and lower with every decade after.[^hearing]

Lesson 1 told how G. W. Pierce's apparatus at Harvard turned the calls of Donald Griffin's bats into clicks in 1938. Today a pocket box does the same job for less than a pair of binoculars, and most of the bat detectors carried on bat walks work the same way: the **heterodyne** detector. It does not record anything and does not slow anything down. It takes a sound at 45 kHz and, as the bat flies, makes a sound at 3 kHz out of it, using only a few components and a dial.

It is worth a minute's thought before reading on. Slowing a recording lowers its pitch, but a live sound cannot be slowed down without falling ever further behind the bat, so the detector needs some other way to turn one frequency into another.

The answer was found for radio, forty years before anyone listened to a bat. In 1901 Reginald Fessenden, a Canadian engineer working on wireless telegraphy, faced the same problem. A transmitter that sends a smooth, continuous radio wave is easier to build and tune than the spark transmitters of the day, but its wave oscillates tens of thousands of times a second or more, and switching it on and off for Morse code gives an operator's headphones nothing to sound but a faint thump at each dot and dash.

Fessenden's idea was to make a second wave inside the receiver, at a slightly different frequency, and combine the two. Where they combine, a new wave appears at the difference between them. Set the receiver's own wave 1,000 cycles a second away from the station's and the headphones sing at 1,000 cycles a second, a clear tone that starts and stops with the code. He called the method **heterodyne**, from the Greek for "other" and "force", and patented it in 1902.[^fessenden] It became practical once vacuum tubes could make a steady wave in the receiver, in the 1910s, and in Edwin Armstrong's superheterodyne of 1918 it went into nearly every radio set made in the twentieth century.
A heterodyne bat detector is Fessenden's receiver with a microphone in place of the aerial. The bat sends the wave; the detector makes the other one, at a frequency set by its dial.

Two notes close in pitch, played together, wobble. A piano tuner hears it when two strings meant to sound the same note are slightly apart: the sound swells and fades a few times a second, and the number of swells each second is the difference between the two frequencies. The two waves drift in and out of step, adding where they agree and cancelling where they oppose. Tuners turn the peg until the wobble slows to nothing.

Adding two ultrasonic waves gives the same wobble, but nothing you can hear: the waves themselves are still at 45 and 48 kHz, and the ear never responds to them, however they swell and fade. A detector has to do something stronger than adding. Its **mixer** multiplies the two signals, moment by moment. Multiplying two waves gives exactly two new waves, one at the difference of their frequencies and one at their sum.[^trig] A call at 45 kHz multiplied by the detector's own 48 kHz becomes a wave at 3 kHz and a wave at 93 kHz. The 3 kHz wave is a real tone that a speaker can play.

The detector's own wave comes from a **local oscillator**, a circuit that makes a steady wave at a frequency set by the dial. After the mixer, a **low-pass filter** passes the low frequencies and blocks the high ones. It throws away the sum, and it throws away any difference above about 5 kHz. So the detector hears only calls within about 5 kHz either side of the dial: a window 10 kHz wide that the dial moves up and down the range of bat calls.

A bat's search call is not a steady note. Lesson 3 described the two shapes: most bats, and every bat in Washington, make **frequency-modulated** (FM) calls, sweeps that fall steeply from a high frequency and then flatten out, all in a few milliseconds. As the sweep falls through the window, the difference between call and dial drops from 5 kHz toward zero and climbs again on the other side. That happens in a millisecond or two, so what comes out is a tick.

blocks.caption: A heterodyne detector at work. Top, a call sweeping down past the dial, drawn slowed right down; the green band is the window the detector hears. Middle, the two waves the mixer makes. Bottom, what reaches the speaker. Listen plays ten calls through the detector at real speed. The calls are synthesised from typical values.
blocks.task: Tune the dial to hear the Myotis at its loudest

blocks.text: Where along the sweep the dial sits changes the sound. Tuned high, on the steep part, the sweep crosses the window in a fraction of a millisecond and the tick is dry and thin. Tuned near the bottom, where the call flattens out and lingers, the call stays in the window for half its length or more, and each tick grows into a fuller, wetter "tock". That frequency, where the call is flattest, is its **characteristic frequency**, and the dial setting where the bat sounds loudest is a rough reading of it. Myotis hunting over water sound best between 40 and 50 kHz. Big brown and silver-haired bats sound best near 25 to 30 kHz, and a little brown bat tuned in at 25 kHz simply vanishes.

The ticks also carry rhythm, which a detector gives you without any tuning. A bat cruising in search of insects ticks about ten times a second, once for each wingbeat. When it closes on a midge the ticks speed up and run together into the rasp of the feeding buzz that lesson 4 explained, the clearest sign on a detector that a bat has just caught something.

parts.title: A whistle that does not stop

blocks.text: The other shape of call is the constant-frequency (CF) call of the horseshoe bats of Europe, Asia and Africa: a single note held for tens of milliseconds, with a short sweep at each end. There are no CF bats in Washington, but the way a detector handles one shows the mixing more plainly than any sweep.

blocks.caption: A greater horseshoe bat's call, a steady 83 kHz, through the same detector. Guess first, then move the dial. Listen plays it at real speed; the calls are synthesised.

blocks.text: A steady call gives a steady difference, so the speaker whistles for as long as the call lasts, then gives a short chirp as the final sweep falls through the window. Bring the dial closer and the whistle drops; set it on the call and the whistle sinks to a flutter and stops. That point is **zero beat**, and it is how a listener, or a piano tuner, reads a frequency to a small fraction of the window. With a horseshoe bat flying toward the microphone, the whistle also rises slightly, because the call reaches the detector raised by the Doppler shift of lesson 5.[^doppler]

Every piece of a heterodyne detector is an ordinary part, and the whole thing fits on a small breadboard, the plug-in board for building circuits without solder that the Circuitry course uses throughout. In order from the bat:

blocks.caption: A heterodyne bat detector as six blocks, with the signal at each step for a 45 kHz call and the dial at 48 kHz. Purple marks the call, green what it becomes after mixing.

blocks.text: The **microphone** has to hear ultrasound. Cheap electret capsules fall off above about 20 kHz but still pick up a loud bat at a few metres; the small MEMS microphones made for phones, sold mounted on breakout boards, often hear well into bat frequencies. The **preamplifier**, an op-amp or two, raises the signal from about a millivolt by a hundred times or more; the op-amp has to be fast enough to amplify 50 kHz by that much, which rules out the slowest old types.

The **mixer** can be a single chip. The NE602, also sold as the SA612, was made for radio receivers and holds a multiplier and its own oscillator in eight pins. A cheaper route uses a CD4066 analogue switch, which connects and disconnects the signal in time with a square wave: switching a signal on and off is multiplying it by one and zero, and it mixes almost as well.[^square] The **oscillator** that drives it can be a 555 timer or the voltage-controlled oscillator in a CD4046, tuned by a potentiometer, which becomes the dial; the Synthesizers course explains how such oscillators work. A resistor and a capacitor make the **low-pass filter**, and an LM386, a small amplifier chip that runs from a 9-volt battery, drives a speaker or headphones.
The dial needs marking in kilohertz. A multimeter with a frequency range, clipped to the oscillator's output, does it in a few minutes: read the frequency at each mark on the knob and write it down.

blocks.title: Outside
points: Go to open water in a park between May and September, starting about 20 minutes after sunset. Set the dial near 45 kHz and point the microphone over the water: Myotis come as quick, dry ticks.
Turn the dial down to about 27 kHz and point it along the tops of the trees. Big brown and silver-haired bats tick more slowly and sound deeper and fuller.
Listen for runs of ticks that speed up into a rasp. Each one is an attempt at an insect, and a bat over a lake can make several a minute.
Note the dial setting where each bat sounds loudest. The next lesson shows how to read the whole call, not a 10 kHz slice of it.

blocks.caption: Five questions on heterodyne detectors
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A heterodyne detector's dial is at 40 kHz and a bat calls a steady 43 kHz. What comes out of the speaker?
choices: A steady tone at about 3 kHz
A tone at 4.3 kHz, the call slowed ten times
Nothing, since 43 kHz is above hearing
A tone at 83 kHz that the filter weakens
items.why: The mixer makes the difference (3 kHz) and the sum (83 kHz). The filter blocks the sum and passes the difference, which is low enough to hear.

items.ask: Why does a heterodyne detector's mixer multiply the call by its own tone instead of adding the two together?
choices: Multiplying makes a real wave at the difference frequency; adding only makes the inaudible waves swell and fade
Adding would make the call louder than the speaker can handle
Multiplying slows the call down, as a recording played at a tenth of its speed does
Adding the two waves would cancel the call completely
items.why: The product of two waves is the sum of two new waves, at their difference and their sum. Adding leaves the original ultrasonic waves, which only beat in loudness.

items.ask: A bat's FM call sweeps from 85 down to 40 kHz in 5 ms. Why does it come out of a heterodyne detector as a short tick?
choices: The sweep passes through the detector's 10 kHz window in a millisecond or two
The detector only switches on for the first millisecond of each call
The low-pass filter shortens every sound to a click
The detector plays only the loudest instant of each call
items.why: The detector hears only calls within about 5 kHz of the dial. A sweep falls through that band quickly, so only a brief piece of each call comes out.

items.ask: With the dial set to 25 kHz, a Myotis calls with a sweep from 85 down to 40 kHz. What do you hear?
choices: Nothing, because the call never comes within 5 kHz of the dial
A faint tick at the end of each call
A steady whistle at about 15 kHz
The full sweep, but quieter
items.why: The call stays above 35 kHz, more than 5 kHz from the dial, so every difference it makes is too high for the filter. Turning down to big brown frequencies loses the Myotis.

items.ask: A home-built detector mixes with a square wave from a 555 timer set to 15 kHz. A Myotis calls near 45 kHz. What happens?
choices: It may be heard, because a square wave also contains a wave at three times its frequency
It cannot be heard, because 45 kHz is 30 kHz from the dial
It is heard as a 30 kHz tone, which is too high for the speaker
It is heard only if the oscillator is changed to a sine wave
items.why: A square wave is a sum of sine waves at its frequency and its odd multiples. Its 45 kHz part mixes with the call, so a square-wave detector also listens at three times its dial.

hearing.title: Who can hear a bat
hearing.text: Young children can hear up to about 20 kHz, and the limit falls with age, to around 12 to 15 kHz for many adults. A few bats call low enough for some people to hear: the spotted bat of eastern Washington near 10 kHz, and the lowest calls and social calls of the hoary bat. Many bats also make audible squeaks in their roosts.

fessenden.title: Reginald Fessenden
fessenden.text: Fessenden, born in Quebec in 1866, worked for Thomas Edison before turning to radio. On Christmas Eve 1906, by the usual account, he broadcast speech and music from Brant Rock, Massachusetts, to ships at sea. His heterodyne receiver had to wait for a steady oscillator inside the receiver; early versions used a small alternator.

trig.title: Why multiplying gives sum and difference
trig.text: It follows from a rule of trigonometry: cos *A* × cos *B* = ½ cos(*A* − *B*) + ½ cos(*A* + *B*). With *A* the call at 45 kHz and *B* the oscillator at 48 kHz, the product is half a wave at 3 kHz plus half a wave at 93 kHz. A real mixer also lets a little of each input through, which the filter removes with the sum.

doppler.title: How far the whistle moves
doppler.text: A bat flying straight at the microphone at 5 metres a second raises its call by 5/343 of itself, about 1.2 kHz at 83 kHz. With the dial at 80 kHz, the whistle rises from 3 kHz to about 4.2 as the bat comes in and drops to about 1.8 as it flies away.

square.title: Square waves and their multiples
square.text: A square wave is a sum of sine waves at its own frequency and at three, five, seven times it, each weaker than the last. A detector that mixes with one also hears calls near three times its dial, more faintly. Builders either accept it, filter the square wave toward a sine wave, or use a mixer such as the NE602 that takes a sine wave.
